posts.on_image: WHAT, ARE YOU PAYING THE GAS BILL NOW?
posts.caption: Our thermostat lived in the hallway, and it belonged to Dad the same way the car keys did. He set it at 66 in October and that was the law until Easter. If you were cold, you were told to put on a sweater, and if you already had a sweater on, you were told to put on another one. My brother Dale once nudged it up to 70 at six in the morning, figuring nobody would know. Dad came down the stairs, didn't say good morning, and walked straight to that dial like he heard the furnace kick on from his bed. He probably did. Dale wore two flannel shirts to school the rest of that week.
posts.first:
We had the round brass kind with the little window in the middle, and Dad could read it from the far end of the hall. I'm in my sixties now and I still feel a little guilty touching mine.

posts.topic: canned cranberry sauce with the ridges
posts.on_image: IF IT DIDN'T HAVE THE RIDGES FROM THE CAN, IT WASN'T CRANBERRY SAUCE.
posts.caption: Every Thanksgiving somebody got the job of opening the cranberry sauce, and at our house that was me. You cut the lid off both ends, held the can over Mom's relish dish, and pushed. If you did it right, it slid out in one shiny piece with every ridge still on it and landed with a sound I can still hear. Aunt Bev brought the homemade kind one year, with whole berries and orange peel in it. It was very nice. It also went home with her almost full. Grandpa sliced the canned one right along the ridges, like they were put there for that reason, and as far as he was concerned they were.
posts.first:
Mom always set it on the cut glass dish from her wedding, like it was something fancy. Nobody touched that dish the other 364 days of the year.

posts.on_image: THE TV REPAIRMAN / $12.50 AND A NEW TUBE / DAD / ONE GOOD SMACK.
posts.caption: When the picture on our Zenith started rolling, Dad got up out of his chair like he'd been called to the front. He'd fool with the vertical hold knob for a minute, mumbling. If that didn't fix it, he'd stand beside the cabinet, size it up, and give the side one good whack with the flat of his hand. Nine times out of ten the picture snapped right back, and he'd sit down like a man who just landed a plane. The tenth time, Mom called the repairman, who showed up in a gray shirt with a case full of tubes and charged us twelve dollars and fifty cents. Dad always said he could have done that. He never once tried.
posts.first:
Our repairman was Mr. Kowalski, and he'd test the old tubes on the machine at the drugstore before he sold you a new one. Dad stood behind him the whole time with his arms folded, supervising.

posts.topic: Dad's 4 AM vacation departure to beat the traffic
posts.on_image: WE LEAVE AT 4 A.M. TO BEAT THE TRAFFIC.
posts.caption: The summer we drove to Panama City Beach, Dad had the station wagon packed the night before, with the suitcases tied on the roof under a tarp and the cooler already in the back. His plan was to leave at four in the morning and beat the traffic, and he announced it at supper like he'd cracked a secret code. At ten till four he flipped on our bedroom light, already dressed, keys in his hand. I walked out barefoot in my pajamas, hugging my pillow, and stood there squinting at him while my sister Connie climbed in the back without ever opening her eyes. Mom came out last with a thermos of coffee and the look of a woman doing some serious thinking about her choices. There wasn't another car on the road until Alabama. Dad said that proved it worked, and he told that part of the story for the next twenty years.
posts.first:
Mom packed bologna sandwiches in wax paper the night before so we wouldn't lose time stopping for lunch. Dad checked his watch at every gas station like we were running a train, and if you weren't back in the car in five minutes you heard about it in the next county.

posts.on_image: SHAKING IT NEVER HELPED. WE ALL SHOOK IT ANYWAY.
posts.caption: The instant camera came out at my cousin Linda's eighth birthday, and the whole party stopped. Uncle Ray aimed it at the cake, it buzzed, and out slid a square of murky gray nothing. Then every adult in the room started waving it around like they were trying to put out a match. Aunt Marge said you had to keep it warm, so she stuck it under her arm. Somebody else said never touch the front, and Grandpa had already touched the front. Ten of us stood around that kitchen table, leaning in, watching a cake slowly show up out of the fog. By the time the candles finally appeared, the real ones had been out for five minutes.
posts.first:
Our family albums have a whole stretch from about '77 to '81 where every picture is a little square with a fat white bottom. Mom wrote the date on each one in ballpoint, and you can still feel the dent from the back.
